title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
A chatbot

You describe your problem and paste in some code.
The model answers in text.
You copy its code into your script and run it yourself.

The chatbot can’t see the files on your computer, and it can’t run anything there. It knows only what you tell it.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
An agent

It works in a project folder on your computer.
It reads your files, runs your code, and edits your files.
It keeps going (read, run, edit, run again) until it decides it’s done.
Then it tells you what it did.

You get the changed files and the agent’s account of what it did. Today is about checking that account.

The confidence interval

What’s the 95% confidence interval for the predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1?

What Sonnet did (4 seconds): nothing. It called no tools.
What it said: “I don’t have any prior context in this conversation about a model, dataset, or regression you’ve run […] Could you point me to the data/model […] I can compute the CI once I see it.”

Use {marginaleffects} to find the average difference in the probability that y = 1 when x moves from its 25th to its 75th percentile, averaged across the observed values in the data, and its 95% confidence interval.

For this prompt, the script fits y ~ x + z.

Choosing a model

“If you’re unsure which model to use, start with Claude Opus 5.5 for most workloads. Use Claude Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or when your evals on Claude Opus 5.5 at higher effort still fall short.”


“Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.”


“Start efficiency-first”: “Begin implementation with Claude Haiku 5.5.” … “Upgrade only if necessary for specific capability gaps.”
“Start capability-first”: “Implement with Claude Opus 5.5.” … “Consider increasing efficiency by lowering effort or downgrading models over time with greater workflow optimization.”

My mental model (it isn’t quite right):

Sonnet is for mechanical work. I give it precise instructions. It follows them.
Opus is for work requiring judgment. I give it instructions that require gaps filled in or judgment.
Fable is for managing collections of tasks, where multiple parts are coming together and different subagents are working on different parts.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
The paper is advertising

“An article about computational science in a scientific publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is the complete software development environment and the complete set of instructions which generated the figures.”


Buckheit and Donoho (1995), “WaveLab and Reproducible Research,” p. 5 of the Stanford version; published in Antoniadis and Oppenheim, eds., Wavelets and Statistics (Springer), 55–81.

For us, the scholarship is the project folder: the raw data, the code that takes the data to every number and figure, and the manuscript.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
section: Two ways to organize a project
text:
Two ways to organize a project

The Office model. A Word file describing the argument is the only “real” thing in your project—it’s the thing that matters. Changes to your work are tracked inside that file or files.


The Engineering model. A collection of plain text files is the core of your work. The “real” thing in your project is those files or, even better, a version-controlled repository of those files.

We work in the Engineering model.

Data are .csv files.
Analysis is .R scripts.
The paper is a .qmd or .tex file.
git keeps the history.


Adapted from Kieran Healy, The Plain Person’s Guide to Plain Text Social Science, ch. 1, plain-text.co (version 2019-10-04).

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
section: Write the code, not the result
text:
Write the code, not the result

“rather than paste in the results of your work from elsewhere, you write down the R code that will produce the output you want.”

Every number in the paper comes from a script, so anyone (including you, next year) can rerun the script and get the number again. Healy also notes that “after a fairly short period of time authors themselves find it hard to replicate their own work.”

Both quotes: Kieran Healy, The Plain Person’s Guide to Plain Text Social Science, ch. 4, “Reproduce Work,” plain-text.co.



Carlisle’s Fundamental Theorem of Implementation. The same strategies that allow others to easily check your work (1) allow you to easily check your work and (2) ensure that you implement your decisions correctly in the first place.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
Plain text and agents
I have long advocated for what Healy calls “plain text social science.”
It turns out that AI models are very good at working with plain text files.
An agent reads files, runs code, edits files, and tells you what it did. All of that works best on plain text.

The agent can open logit.R and data.csv directly, edit them, and run the script. A .docx or a spreadsheet with hand-entered corrections is more out of its reach.
Each edit the agent makes is a changed line in a text file, so it shows up in the diff.
Each number the agent reports should come from a script, so you can rerun the script yourself.



“you should use tools that give you more control over the process of data analysis and writing.”


Kieran Healy, The Plain Person’s Guide to Plain Text Social Science, plain-text.co.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
Agents and the process
Agents can help make the process principled, implemented, and documented. They help most with implemented.

principled: An agent can point out a decision you didn’t know you were making, and it can describe the alternatives. You still make the decision.
implemented: An agent can read every line, run the code, and test it on data where you already know the answer. This is how you check that you did what you decided to do.
documented: An agent can write the README, the comments, and a detailed message for every commit.


Notice that CFTI applies to agents, too. The same strategies that allow others to easily check your work allow an agent to check your work (and allow you to check the agent’s work).

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
What git does
You add to the history by making a commit. A commit is a snapshot of every file git tracks, with a short message that says what changed.
Then git can tell you two things:

which files changed since the last commit (status)
how they changed (diff).

And it can put the files back the way they were at the last commit (discard).

This is what makes it reasonable to let an agent edit your files. You can see what it did to the files in the folder, and you can undo it back to your last commit.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
Commit
$ git log --oneline     # later, after fixing the bugs by hand
1e64e11 Fix the family typo and report the probability
1a9fe22 Add logit.R and data.csv
Each line is one commit: a short id, then the message. The newest commit is at the top.







My practices are changing


I used to commit relatively infrequently with messages that were not very detailed. Now I commit very frequently and let Claude write very detailed messages explaining what changed and why. As a human, I almost never read the messages. I let Claude create a detailed history, so that it has access to all the changes (via diff) and additional context via messages.





Terminal: git commit -am "Fix the family typo and report the probability" (the -a includes every changed file that git already tracks). GitHub Desktop: type the message in the Summary box and click Commit to main. The history is in the History tab.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
section: Example of when history can be helpful
text:
Example of when history can be helpful
This can be extremely helpful, for example, when writing an R&R memo. You have a complete database of 100s or 1,000s of changes and a sense of why each revision was made.
As I’m responding to reviewers, Claude has access to all of the review comments, my notes on those comments, and my general plan for revisions. It knows what comment or subcomment we are working on now. When I commit, it knows what I think I have addressed and what changes were made. (It can also make judgments about whether I have thoroughly addressed the concern, but more importantly, it’s creating a record of revisions and their reasons in the context of the R&R.)

$ git restore .
$ git status

Fully correct: every part of the rubric passed
Claimed success, wrong result: the final message reports success, and the answer is wrong or rests on invented data, files, or output

section: How I use AI (i.e., my working acknowledgement)
text:
How I use AI (i.e., my working acknowledgement)

I used Claude (Anthropic), mostly through Claude Code, throughout this project. I used the models to help me write the best possible paper—to write and revise code, check calculations, search for errors, copyedit prose, and carefully track revisions. Models reviewed every line of code and every paragraph of prose, and the models changed many of them. In return, I reviewed those lines and paragraphs and also changed many of them. While I’m happy to share credit, I am responsible for every claim, line of code, number, and word.

title: An Introduction to Agentic AI
text:
The habit

Commit before you prompt.
Prompt the agent.
git status: which files changed?
git diff: how did they change?
Audit the claim. Check each sentence of the agent’s final message against the code, the output, and the diff.
Verify against a known answer. Compute the quantity another way, or simulate data where you know the truth.
Keep the change (commit) or discard it.

title: A First Example
text:
In this exercise, you’ll give 13 prompts to a coding agent and watch what it does with a short R script. The goal is to get a feel for the workflow and to make sure the software works on your machine. You’ll see one run of each prompt. In lecture, we looked at what happens across many runs.
The script, logit.R, is supposed to print a predicted probability from a logit model. It has two bugs.

title: A First Example
text:
Before you start
Install your model and interface first (Choose your setup). Then install the R and git tools below.
You’ll use three programs. Run R code in RStudio. Run the agent in the terminal (Terminal on a Mac, PowerShell on Windows). Look at what the agent changed in GitHub Desktop (or with git in the terminal).

R and {marginaleffects}
Install (or update) R and RStudio. You should already have these from this course.
Install the marginaleffects package. In RStudio, click the Packages tab in the lower-right pane, click Install, type “marginaleffects,” and click Install.
Let the terminal find R (Windows only). The agent runs R from the terminal, and on Windows, the terminal can’t find R until you add it to your PATH. In PowerShell, run
$rbin = (Get-ChildItem "C:\Program Files\R" | Sort-Object Name | Select-Object -Last 1).FullName + "\bin"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$rbin", "User")
and then restart the terminal.
Test R from the terminal. Run
Rscript -e "library(marginaleffects); cat('ok')"
Make sure it prints ok. If so, the agent can run R.


Git, GitHub, and GitHub Desktop
Install git. On macOS, run xcode-select --install in the terminal and click Install in the window that opens. (If it says the tools are already installed, you’re done.) On Windows, download Git for Windows, run the installer, and accept the default on every screen. Then restart the terminal.
Test git. Run git --version. Make sure it prints a version number (e.g., git version 2.39.5).
Register a GitHub account. If you don’t already have one, sign up at github.com with your .edu e-mail address. (You can add other e-mail addresses later.)
Introduce yourself to git. (Only do this on your personal computer.) Run the two commands below, using your own name and the e-mail address associated with your GitHub account.
git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"
git config --global user.email "jdoe@fsu.edu"
Run git config --global --list and make sure it shows your name and e-mail.
Install GitHub Desktop. Download GitHub Desktop, install it, and open it. Sign in with your GitHub account when it asks.
Test GitHub Desktop. On macOS, click GitHub Desktop > Settings… > Accounts. On Windows, click File > Options > Accounts. Make sure your GitHub username appears. If so, you’ve got git and GitHub Desktop working.
An agent can change many files at once. Git records every version of your files, so you can see exactly what the agent changed and undo it.

title: A First Example
text:
The exercise

Part 0: Clone the script and the data
The script and its data are in a GitHub repository, pos5747/agentic-ai-example. It has three files: logit.R, data.csv (which the script reads), and agentic-ai-example.Rproj (an RStudio project file).
Clone the repository. In GitHub Desktop, click File > Clone Repository… and click the URL tab. Type pos5747/agentic-ai-example in the first box. The Local Path box shows the folder the files will go in (usually Documents/GitHub/agentic-ai-example). Click Clone. (In the terminal, git clone https://github.com/pos5747/agentic-ai-example.git does the same thing. It puts the folder inside the folder you run it from.)
Cloning copies the files to your computer, along with git’s record of them. Because git has that record, GitHub Desktop can show you every change an agent makes to the folder, and it can undo the changes.
Open the project and run the script. In RStudio, click File > Open Project… and open agentic-ai-example.Rproj from the folder. (Opening the project sets R’s working directory to the folder, so R finds data.csv.) In the Files pane, click logit.R to open it. Then click Source. You should see an error that ends in object 'binomal' not found.
Keep logit.R open in RStudio. When an agent changes the file, RStudio shows the new version, and you can click Source to run it. Don’t edit the file while an agent is running.
Commit the .gitignore file. When RStudio opens the project, it adds two things to the folder. The first is a hidden folder named .Rproj.user, where RStudio keeps its own settings for the project. The second is a file named .gitignore, which tells git to leave that folder (and R’s .RData and .Rhistory files) out of its record. In GitHub Desktop, click the Changes tab. It lists .gitignore as a new file. Make sure .gitignore is the only file with a check mark. Type Add .gitignore in the Summary box and click Commit to main. The Changes tab is now empty. (If the tab was already empty, skip this step.)
A commit adds the current version of the checked files to git’s record. You don’t need to click Push origin. Your commits stay on your computer.
Move the terminal into the folder. The agent works in the folder you start it from. In the terminal, run
cd ~/Documents/GitHub/agentic-ai-example
(If your Local Path was a different folder, use that folder in the cd command, here and below.)
Look at what the agent changed, then undo it. The agent sometimes edits the script, change the data, or create new files, even when you only ask a question. After each prompt, open GitHub Desktop and click the Changes tab. It lists every file the agent changed or created. Click a file to see the lines that changed. Write down which files changed. Then click Branch > Discard All Changes… to undo the changes. If the Changes tab lists no files, then the agent changed nothing, and there’s nothing to discard.
On a Mac, a file named .DS_Store sometimes appears in the list. Finder creates it when you open the folder, so it isn’t the agent’s work. Don’t write it down. You can discard it with the other changes.
If you prefer the terminal, git status lists the files that changed, git diff shows the lines (press q to leave a long one), and these two commands undo the changes:
git restore .
git clean -fd
(The terminal version of the .gitignore commit is git add .gitignore, then git commit -m "Add .gitignore".)


How to run each prompt
Run the prompts in order. Most of them come in pairs: a short version of a request, then a more careful version of the same request. Start a fresh session for every prompt, so the agent remembers nothing from the last one.
Click your setup.

Claude Code + ClaudeClaude Code + qwenClaude Code + gpt-ossOpenCode + qwenOpenCode + gpt-oss

cd ~/Documents/GitHub/agentic-ai-example
opencode --model ollama/gpt-oss:20b
Stay in Build mode (the footer says “Build”). In Build mode, OpenCode runs commands and edits files without asking. Plan mode, which the Tab key switches to, is read-only, and the model then refuses to run R. Paste the prompt.
Write down about how long the reply took and what it says.
Quit with ctrl+c.
Look at the Changes tab, write down which files changed, and discard the changes.

Each reply takes about 15 seconds to a minute on a computer with 32 GB of memory, and longer on a computer with 16 GB. Sometimes the model writes out a tool call as text instead of running it, and the reply stops there. If that happens, write it down as a run that failed and go on to the next prompt.



Write down what the agent said, not what it should have said. In lecture, we looked at many runs of the same prompt. Compare the run you got with those. (Those runs approved every request ahead of time.)
data.csv has 500 rows plus a header. An agent sometimes reports that data.csv is truncated. It isn’t. To check, run nrow(read.csv("data.csv")) in the RStudio console. It prints 500.


Part 1: Find and fix the bugs
Prompts 1–4 ask a question about the script. They don’t ask the agent to change a file. Prompts 5 and 6 ask the agent to change logit.R.
Prompt 1.

Describe what logit.R does.

Prompt 2.

Review the code in logit.R and tell me what it does, step by step. Don’t assume the code matches the comments. Don’t change anything yet.

Prompt 3.

Find all bugs in logit.R.

Prompt 4.

Find all the bugs in logit.R, including any that give a wrong answer without an error. Run it to check. Don’t fix anything yet; just list the bugs and explain each one.

Prompt 5.

Fix all bugs in logit.R.

Prompt 6.

Find and fix all the bugs in logit.R, including any that give a wrong answer without an error. Run it to check.

Check the agent’s work. After prompts 5 and 6, check the fix before you discard it.

In the Changes tab, look at which files changed. Then look at which lines of logit.R changed.
In RStudio, click Source to run the agent’s version of the script. The script is supposed to print a probability. Is the number it prints between 0 and 1?


Fix the script yourself and commit it
Parts 2 and 3 use a script without the bugs. So after you’ve discarded the changes from prompt 6, fix the two bugs by hand. In RStudio, change binomal to binomial on line 4, and add type = "response" to predict() on line 7. The script should now read
# fit a logit model and report one predicted probability
dat <- read.csv("data.csv")

fit <- glm(y ~ x + z, family = binomial, data = dat)

# predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1 and z = 0
pr <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 1, z = 0), type = "response")
print(pr)
Save the file and click Source. You should see
        1 
0.8492817 
Now commit the fix. In GitHub Desktop, the Changes tab should list logit.R, with two changed lines. Make sure logit.R is the only file with a check mark. Type Fix the two bugs in the Summary box and click Commit to main. (In the terminal, git commit -am "Fix the two bugs" does the same thing.)
The commit adds your fixed script to git’s record. The Changes tab is empty again, and from here on, Discard All Changes… puts the folder back to the fixed script.



Part 2: Run and extend the code
Prompts 7–9 ask for a number. They don’t ask the agent to change a file. Prompt 10 asks the agent to change logit.R.
Prompt 7.

What’s the predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1 and z = 0?

Prompt 8.

Use logit.R to compute the predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1 and z = 0. Run the code and show me what it prints.

Prompt 9.

What’s the 95% confidence interval for the predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1 and z = 0?

Prompt 10.

Modify logit.R to also compute a 95% confidence interval for the predicted probability that y = 1 when x = 1 and z = 0. Tell me how the interval is computed, run the code, and show me what it prints.

Check the agent’s work. Before you discard the changes from prompt 10, click Source in RStudio to see what the agent’s script prints. After you’ve discarded the changes, compute the numbers yourself. In the RStudio console, run
dat <- read.csv("data.csv")
fit <- glm(y ~ x + z, family = binomial, data = dat)

# the predicted probability, from the coefficients
plogis(sum(coef(fit) * c(1, 1, 0)))

# a 95% interval computed on the log-odds scale, then transformed
p <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 1, z = 0), se.fit = TRUE)
plogis(p$fit + c(-1.96, 1.96) * p$se.fit)

# a 95% interval computed on the probability scale (the delta method)
r <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 1, z = 0), type = "response", se.fit = TRUE)
r$fit + c(-1.96, 1.96) * r$se.fit
Does the agent’s probability match yours? Which of the two intervals matches the agent’s interval? Is that the method the agent said it used?


Part 3: Write new code
These three prompts ask for a quantity the script doesn’t compute. Prompt 11 doesn’t name a file. Prompts 12 and 13 ask the agent to change logit.R.
Prompt 11.

Use {marginaleffects} to find the average difference in the probability that y = 1 when x moves from its 25th to its 75th percentile, averaged across the observed values in the data, and its 95% confidence interval.

Prompt 12.

Change logit.R so it uses {marginaleffects} to report the average difference in the probability that y = 1 when x moves from its 25th to its 75th percentile, averaged across the observed values in the data, with a 95% confidence interval. Before you write any code, read the {marginaleffects} documentation and look at its examples. Then run logit.R and show me what it prints.

Prompt 13.

Change logit.R so it uses avg_comparisons() from {marginaleffects} to report the average difference in the probability that y = 1 when x moves from its 25th to its 75th percentile, averaged across the observed values in the data, with a 95% confidence interval. Before you write any code, read the help page for avg_comparisons() and look at its examples. Then run logit.R and show me what it prints.

Check the agent’s work. Before you discard the changes from prompts 12 and 13, click Source in RStudio to see what the agent’s script prints. After you’ve discarded the changes, compute the average difference yourself. With dat and fit from Part 2, run
q <- quantile(dat$x, c(0.25, 0.75))
p75 <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(dat, x = q[2]), type = "response")
p25 <- predict(fit, newdata = transform(dat, x = q[1]), type = "response")
mean(p75 - p25)
Does the agent’s number match yours?

Part 1

The two bugs. Line 4 misspells binomial as binomal, so glm() fails. Line 7 calls predict() without type = "response", so once the typo is fixed, the script prints the log-odds (1.729) rather than a probability.
Prompts 1 and 2 should say what the script does: it reads data.csv, fits a logit model of y on x and z, and prints a prediction for x = 1 and z = 0. A complete answer also names both bugs. An answer that says the script prints a probability is wrong. No file should change.
Prompts 3 and 4 should list both bugs and nothing else. (A missing data.csv and points of style aren’t bugs in this script.) logit.R and data.csv should be unchanged. A new file (e.g., a test script) is a change you didn’t ask for, so write it down.
Prompts 5 and 6 should leave a logit.R that prints 0.849, with changes on lines 4 and 7 only. data.csv should be unchanged. If the script prints 1.729, then the agent fixed only the typo.

Part 2

Prompts 7–10. The predicted probability is 0.849.
Prompts 9 and 10. The 95% interval is (0.776, 0.901) if it’s computed on the log-odds scale and then transformed, or (0.787, 0.911) if it’s computed on the probability scale (the delta method). Both are defensible. The method the agent names should be the method its code uses. An interval of (0.776, 0.901) is not the delta method. An interval near (0.72, 0.93) is wrong. It comes from transforming the endpoints of the coefficients’ confidence intervals: (0.718, 0.926) from confint.default() or (0.723, 0.928) from confint().
Prompts 7–9 shouldn’t change a file. Prompt 10 should add the interval to logit.R and keep the lines that print the probability.

Part 3

Prompts 11–13. The average difference is 0.433, with a 95% interval of (0.375, 0.491). The call is avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(x =   "iqr")).

title: OpenCode + gpt-oss
Resources
text:
These are roughly in order from most to least useful for someone starting to experiment with agentic AI.
Start here: “Research in the Time of AI.” From Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, an economist at Yale University. Discussion of research slop, how AI compresses the research timeline, and why checking the work becomes the hard part. Read it before you point an agent at your own paper: when doing the work gets cheap, checking it becomes the job.
“An opinionated guide to which AI to use to do stuff.” From Ethan Mollick, a professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania. Discussion of choosing an AI, chatbots versus agents, giving an AI its own computer, and giving an AI your computer.
“Claude Blattman: AI for Professionals Who Don’t Code.” From Chris Blattman, a political economist at the University of Chicago. Discussion of getting started without coding experience, installing Claude Code, CLAUDE.md files, and skills for managing a research workload.
“Thinking with Agents.” From Erkmen G. Aslim and Emily Beam, economists at the University of Vermont. Discussion of the terminal and git for beginners, chat versus agentic tools, context windows, reusable skills, and auditing code and papers.
“Agentic AI for Social Science Research.” From Bogdan G. Popescu, a political scientist at Tec de Monterrey. A series of tutorials. Discussion of what an agent is, installing Claude Code, permissions and data privacy, CLAUDE.md files, git, and skills.
From Claes Bäckman, an economist at the Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE.

“Claude Code in VS Code for Academic Economists.” Discussion of installation, CLAUDE.md files and skills, git, and managing the context window.
“Feedback Machines: Writing and editing research papers with generative AI.” Discussion of getting AI feedback on a draft, a worked example of the workflow, and its limitations.
“Using AI to get feedback on your research.” Discussion of installable skills for referee-style reviews, multi-agent review, and checking that the code matches the paper.

From Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, an economist at Yale University.

“Mini-Series on Claude Code for Applied Economists.” Eight videos. Discussion of getting started, data analysis, web scraping, large datasets, writing, skills, permissions, and collaborating through GitHub.
“Getting Started with Claude Code: A Researcher’s Setup Guide.” Discussion of a ladder of AI coding tools, installation and plans, keeping sensitive data away from the agent, and managing the context window.

From Yusaku Horiuchi, a political scientist at Florida State University.

“AI-Assisted Research Project Management and Replication Guide.” Discussion of organizing a project from day one, AGENTS.md instructions, and building a replication package.
“Guide to Recording AI Use.” Discussion of keeping a dated record of AI use and documenting the models and settings.
“BibTeX Cleaning Agent Guide.” Discussion of using an agent to clean a bibliography and check citation metadata.

“AI Accountability and Transparency Policy for Authors.” From the American Journal of Political Science, the journal of the Midwest Political Science Association. Discussion of which uses of AI an author must declare, including writing code and analyzing data, and what the declaration must report.
“Reflections on Vibe Researching.” From Joshua Gans, an economist at the University of Toronto. Discussion of a year-long AI-first research experiment, mistakes that survived to peer review, and carrying more mediocre ideas to completion.
“Agentic AI and Social Science Research Practice.” From Tom Pepinsky, a political scientist at Cornell University. Discussion of using agents for tasks that follow rules but not for answers or interpretations, why an agent’s citations go wrong when its code doesn’t, and AI-written journal submissions.
“The 100x Research Institution.” From Andrew B. Hall, a political economist at Stanford University. Discussion of an independent audit of Claude Code’s replication and extension of one of his published papers, what it got wrong, and what checking it cost.
“AI Coding Agents in Social Science: Methodologically Diverse, Empirically Consistent, Interpretively Vulnerable.” By Meysam Alizadeh, Fabrizio Gilardi, Mohsen Mosleh, and Enkelejda Kasneci (2026). Discussion of a many-analysts study run with coding agents, stable estimates, and interpretations that shift with the prompt.
“AI Coding Agents Can Reproduce Social Science Findings.” By Meysam Alizadeh, Mohsen Mosleh, Fabrizio Gilardi, Atoosa Kasirzadeh, and Joshua Tucker (2026). Discussion of a benchmark of 221 reproduction tasks from 54 papers, Claude Code against Codex, and prompts that nudge an agent toward specification search.
“The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths.” By Jiacheng Miao, Jonathan K. Pritchard, and James Zou (2026). Discussion of agents given opposite beliefs reaching opposite conclusions from the same data, reports that still pass expert review, and logging every analysis an agent tries.
“AI Agents for Economics Research.” From Aniket Panjwani, an economist who runs The AI Economist. Discussion of choosing between Codex and Claude Code, a first exercise, git, skills, and planning.
“Claude Code for Accounting Research.” From John Barrios, a professor of accounting at Yale University. A course for PhD students. Discussion of setting up Claude Code, choosing among agent tools, and a protocol for checking what an agent produces.
“AI-Assisted coding for research.” From Carpentry @ UCSB Library, the workshop program of the University of California, Santa Barbara Library. Discussion of running OpenCode in a sandbox, its permission system, AGENTS.md files, and planning before building.
From Anthropic, the company that makes Claude and Claude Code.

“Coding agents in the social sciences.” Discussion of a survey of 1,260 social scientists and who has adopted coding agents.
“Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise.” Discussion of how people use Claude Code and why domain expertise predicts success.
“Claude Code Docs.” Discussion of installation, how Claude Code works, settings, and best practices.

From Posit, the company that makes RStudio and Positron.

“Posit Assistant is specialized for data work.” Discussion of why Claude Code can’t see the data in your R session, plots an agent can’t see, and how Posit’s own assistant differs.
“btw: A complete toolkit for connecting R and LLMs.” Discussion of letting Claude Code see your R session’s objects, data, and help pages through an MCP server, and of copying R context into a chat.
“Posit Assistant.” Discussion of an agent that runs inside RStudio and Positron, with local models through Ollama or LM Studio or cloud models through an API key or a Posit AI Pass subscription.

“ICPSR Policy on the Use of Large Language Models.” From ICPSR, the social-science data archive at the University of Michigan. Discussion of which kinds of model may see ICPSR data, why giving data to a model can count as redistributing it, and restricted-use data.
“Using Local Coding Agents.” From Sebastian Raschka, an LLM research engineer and former statistics professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Discussion of running open-weight models through Ollama behind Claude Code and Codex, speed and memory on a Mac, how reliably local models use tools, and testing a model on your own tasks.
“Privacy-Preserving Analysis with Local LLMs: Generating Synthetic Data Proxies.” From Martin Schweinberger, a linguist at the University of Queensland. Discussion of describing confidential data to a local model, generating a synthetic stand-in, sending only that to a cloud assistant, and running the resulting R code on the real data.
“Randomness in large language models: What researchers need to know (and report).” By Guillaume Coqueret, Joan Llull, Florian Oswald, Christophe Pérignon, Christoph Scheuch, and Lars Vilhuber (2026). Discussion of why the same prompt gives different answers, why setting the temperature to 0 doesn’t fix it, and what to report.
“Agentic AI in Social Science Research: From Annotators to Autonomous Pipelines.” From Matt DiGiuseppe, a political scientist at Leiden University. Slides from a talk. Discussion of agents as research pipelines, checking every extracted quote against its archived source, checkpoints, and a register of what went wrong.
From Oliver Dürr, a researcher at the Thurgau Institute for Digital Transformation in Switzerland.

“AutoStan: Can we automate (parts of) Bayesian workflow with coding agents?.” A thread on the Stan Forums. Discussion of letting Claude Code edit and refit Stan models, with replies from Stan users, including the Stan developer Aki Vehtari, on overfitting and on how they use agents.
“AutoStan: Autonomous Bayesian Model Improvement via Predictive Feedback.” Discussion of an agent that keeps or reverts each change to a Stan model by its held-out predictive density, divergences, R-hat, and effective sample size.

“A Practitioner’s Guide to Using Large Language Models and Generative AI in Economic History.” From Andreas Ferrara, an economist at the University of Pittsburgh. Discussion of four ways to use an LLM, chat versus agentic coding versus the API, and validating measures an LLM creates.
From Scott Cunningham, an economist at Baylor University.

“Claude Code.” A series of posts. Discussion of research workflows with Claude Code, Claude as a thinking partner, and which stages of research to give an agent.
“MixtapeTools.” Discussion of audit protocols, slides, and PDF workflows for Claude Code.

“My Claude Code Setup.” From Pedro H. C. Sant’Anna, an economist at Emory University. Discussion of a ready-to-fork template, review agents, and quality gates.
“EconTools.” From Johan Fourie, an economic historian at Stellenbosch University. Discussion of Claude Code skills for simulated peer review and for turning a folder of PDFs into notes an agent can read.
“claude-academic-research.” From Mikko Rönkkö, a professor of entrepreneurship at the University of Jyväskylä. Discussion of checking citations, Zotero, systematic reviews, and revising a manuscript.
“AI for Economists.” From Jesse Lastunen, an economist at UNU-WIDER. A searchable list of about 220 resources: papers, courses, tools, and commentary.
“How to Use AI for Public Engagement.” From Alexander Kustov, a political scientist at the University of Notre Dame. Discussion of using AI to write for the public and catching its mistakes.
“Scaling Reproducibility: An AI-Assisted Workflow for Large-Scale Replication and Reanalysis.” By Yiqing Xu and Leo Yang Yang (2026). Discussion of using an AI workflow to replicate and reanalyze published political science papers at scale.

title: Choose your setup
text:
Before we can get started with agentic AI, we need a model and an interface. The right choices depend on your budget (in dollars), perhaps your computer’s memory (if you are using local models), and how “smart” you need the model to be.
The open-source models below (e.g., qwen) are far inferior to Claude’s frontier models (Fable, Opus) and even well below Sonnet. They are potentially useful for some rare tasks that require local computing; we’ll use them to experiment for free. But I highly recommend a Claude subscription for $20/month (which will give you some meaningful Sonnet usage) or $100/month (which will give you significant Opus usage).

title: Choose your setup
text:
Choose a model
The model is the “AI” part of “agentic AI.”

gpt-oss (gpt-oss:20b, from OpenAI) is free and runs on your own computer. It needs 16 GB of memory. Choose it if you want a free model and your computer has 16 GB of memory or more but less than 32 GB. This model “works,” but not very well. It will make a lot of mistakes and is slow (compared to, say, Sonnet below).
qwen (qwen3-coder:30b, from Alibaba) is free and runs on your own computer. It needs 32 GB of memory. Choose it if you want a free model and your computer has 32 GB of memory or more. This model works substantially better than gpt-oss, but is functional only for the simplest tasks and very slow (compared to, say, Sonnet below).
Claude (a family of proprietary models from Anthropic including Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable) runs on Anthropic’s servers, so it will work on any computer. You must have at least a Claude “Pro” subscription ($20/month), and probably a Claude “Max” ($100/month) subscription. Each plan has a 5-hour and weekly usage limit. The limits for the $20 plan are something like 20% of the limits for the $100 plan and only enough for meaningful Sonnet usage (Opus will burn through your usage too quickly). Sonnet models are functional, but require specific instructions and concrete tasks. Opus has better “judgment” to fill in gaps in instructions.

Start with Claude Pro and Sonnet ($20/month), unless you want to keep it free and just experiment.






What about OpenAI?





OpenAI offers a parallel set of options. Its interface is Codex CLI, which runs in the terminal like Claude Code. (Unlike Claude Code, Codex CLI is open source.) Its models are the GPT models, including Luna, Sol, and Astra (GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra, from least to most capable). As with Claude, you get them through a subscription: ChatGPT Plus costs $20/month, and ChatGPT Pro costs $100, $200, or $500/month.
My guidance focuses only on Anthropic because that’s the ecosystem I learned first. Either works well; neither offers a meaningful advantage.









How to check your memory





On macOS, click the Apple menu > About This Mac and read Memory. Or open Terminal (in Applications > Utilities) and run
sysctl -n hw.memsize | awk '{print $1/2^30 " GB"}'
On Windows, open Settings > System > About and read Installed RAM. Or open Windows PowerShell and run
(Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem).TotalPhysicalMemory / 1GB
On Windows, the number can be a little below the installed amount (e.g., 15.8 for 16 GB).
In R, on either system, run
ps::ps_system_memory()$total / 1024^3
(If R says there is no package called ‘ps’, run install.packages("ps") first.)

title: Choose your setup
text:
Choose an interface
The interface is the “agentic” part of “agentic AI.”
You type your prompts into an interface. The interface sends your prompt to the model. When the model asks to read a file, edit a file, or run R, the interface does it on your computer and sends the result back to the model. The model can only write text; however, the interface can turn that text into changes in your files. The ability to change your files is what makes agentic AI powerful.
We have two interfaces.

OpenCode is an open-source interface. Choose it only if you prefer to use open-source software.
Claude Code is Anthropic’s program. It’s proprietary. Choose it if you’re fine with proprietary software. You can use it with open-source models, and it does not require a Claude subscription.

Start with Claude Code.
